claim: TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer according to the International Cancer Genome Consortium.
source: The International Cancer Genome Consortium has recognized that the TP53 gene is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer (Hollstein et al., 1991; Olivier et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hollstein et al., 1991 and Olivier et al., 2010

claim: In most tumors, TP53 point mutations co-occur with loss of one copy of the TP53 gene (LOH) due to deletions in chromosome 17.
source: Genetic studies show that, in most tumors, TP53 point mutations co-occur with the loss of one copy of the TP53 gene (LOH) due to deletions in chromosome 17 where the TP53 locus is located (Baker et al., 1989; Menon et al., 1990; Olivier et al., 2010; Rivlin et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to genetic studies

claim: TP53 has been described as a tumor suppressor gene based on experimental evidence.
source: Consistent with these observations and the two-hit hypothesis proposed by A.G. Knudson, experimental evidences have led to the description of TP53 as a tumor suppressor gene (Knudson, 1971; Baker et al., 1989; Finlay et al., 1989; Donehower et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies and Knudson's two-hit hypothesis

claim: TP53 missense mutations occur more frequently at specific residues (R175, G245, R248, R249, R273 and R282) referred to as 'hotspot' mutation sites.
source: This simplistic vision has been challenged by recent studies spurred by the observation that TP53 missense mutations do not have a uniform distribution; rather, they occur more frequently at specific residues (R175, G245, R248, R249, R273 and R282) often referred to as 'hotspot' TP53 mutation sites (Petitjean et al., 2007; Brosh and Rotter, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Petitjean et al., 2007 and Brosh and Rotter, 2009

claim: Certain p53 missense mutants exhibit gain of function activities during tumorigenesis.
source: Indeed, many lines of evidence have now demonstrated that certain p53 missense mutants could exhibit a gain of function activities during tumorigenesis (Brosh and Rotter, 2009; Oren and Rotter, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Some gain of function p53 mutations (R175H, R248Q, R273H) result in increased cell invasion, migration, proliferation and anti-apoptosis in different in-vitro models.
source: For instance, some of the gain of function mutations, including R175H, R248Q, R273H, resulted in an increase in cell invasion, cell migration, cell proliferation and anti-apoptosis in different in-vitro models (Muller and Vousden, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muller and Vousden, 2014

claim: Mice expressing TP53 R172H and R270H mutations manifest more aggressive and metastatic tumors compared to p53-null mice.
source: Additionally, mice expressing TP53 R172H (human R175H) and R270H (human R273H) mutations manifest a broad spectrum of aggressive tumors that are more metastatic in nature when compared to p53-null mice (Lang et al., 2004; Olive et al., 2004; Doyle et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to mouse model studies

claim: The mechanism of function of p53 gain of function mutants mostly relies on alterations to the p53 transcription program.
source: Though different gain of function mutants exhibit various pro-tumorigenic phenotypes, their mechanism of function mostly relies on alterations to the p53 transcription program (Freed-Pastor and Prives, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Freed-Pastor and Prives, 2012

claim: TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations occur at higher than expected frequencies.
source: In this study, we similarly report that certain TP53 truncating mutations promote tumorigenesis rather than halt it. In fact, we observed that TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations occur at higher than expected frequencies and, when ectopically expressed in cells, induce the acquisition of pro-metastatic features.
evidence: Supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations induce the acquisition of pro-metastatic features when ectopically expressed in cells.
source: In fact, we observed that TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations occur at higher than expected frequencies and, when ectopically expressed in cells, induce the acquisition of pro-metastatic features.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in the manuscript

claim: TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations are necessary for cell survival in normal 2-D cell growing conditions.
source: In contrast to TP53 missense gain of function mutations, we found that TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations are necessary for cell survival in normal 2-D cell growing conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in the manuscript

claim: TP53 exon-6 truncating mutants lack transcriptional activity.
source: As we have shown in this study, these p53 mutants lack transcriptional activity and, instead, have phenotypes that depend on their molecular and functional interactions with Cyclophilin D in the mitochondria.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in the manuscript

claim: TP53 exon-6 truncating mutants have phenotypes that depend on their molecular and functional interactions with Cyclophilin D in the mitochondria.
source: As we have shown in this study, these p53 mutants lack transcriptional activity and, instead, have phenotypes that depend on their molecular and functional interactions with Cyclophilin D in the mitochondria.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in the manuscript

claim: TP53 nonsense mutations are distributed non-randomly with increased frequency in correspondence to TP53 exon-6 in the TCGA cohort.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, it is evident that TP53 nonsense mutations are distributed non-randomly with increased frequency in correspondence to TP53 exon-6 (i.e. TP53 exon-6 nonsense).
evidence: Supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: Nonsense mutations occur at sites distinct from those affected by missense mutations.
source: Interestingly, our analysis also indicated that nonsense mutations occur at sites distinct from those affected by missense mutations (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: The distribution of TP53 nonsense mutations with increased frequency in exon-6 was confirmed in the MSKCC cohort.
source: These findings were confirmed in an independent pan-cancer dataset of 3797 cases, in which targeted sequencing was performed at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (Cheng et al., 2015), referred to here as the 'MSKCC cohort' (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by independent dataset analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: Missense mutations are observed at a frequency 1.9 fold higher than expected in the TCGA cohort.
source: As indicated in Figure 1E, we found that in the case of missense mutations the relative expected frequency was 0.34, while the relative observed frequency was 0.64, based on the analysis of the TCGA cohort. This finding suggests that missense mutations are observed at a frequency that is 1.9 fold higher than expected.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1E

claim: Exon-6 nonsense mutations show a 4-5 fold increase in observed frequency compared to expected frequency.
source: Interestingly, when we limited our analysis only to exon-6 nonsense mutations we found a 4–5 fold increase in the observed frequency compared to the expected frequency (Figure 1C and D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figures 1C, 1D, and supplement

claim: Exon-6 nonsense mutations occur nearly 5 times more frequently than all TP53 mutations (p=3.869e-11).
source: This finding indicates that nonsense mutations in exon-6 occur nearly 5 times more frequently than all TP53 mutations (p=3.869e-11) and 2–3 times more frequently than either missense mutations or nonsense mutations outside of exon-6 (p=3.71e-4 and p=8e-5, respectively).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with p-values

claim: Exon-6 nonsense mutations occur 2-3 times more frequently than either missense mutations or nonsense mutations outside of exon-6.
source: This finding indicates that nonsense mutations in exon-6 occur nearly 5 times more frequently than all TP53 mutations (p=3.869e-11) and 2–3 times more frequently than either missense mutations or nonsense mutations outside of exon-6 (p=3.71e-4 and p=8e-5, respectively).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis with p-values

claim: Overall truncating mutations account for more than 25% of all TP53 mutations in both TCGA and MSKCC datasets.
source: We found that even though nonsense mutations occur at a rate of 13%, overall truncating mutations account for more than 25% of all TP53 mutations in both datasets examined (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data analysis shown in supplementary figure

claim: The distribution of TP53 mutations differs in various tumor types, ranging from 7.3% in multiple myeloma to 94.9% in ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma.
source: We also observed that the distribution of TP53 mutations differs in various tumor types, ranging from 7.3 to 94.9% in the case of multiple myeloma (MM) and ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma (OVCA) respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by data analysis in Supplementary file 1

claim: The frequency of TP53 truncating mutations spans from 1.46% in multiple myeloma to 27.53% in lung squamous cell carcinoma.
source: As for TP53 truncating mutations, their frequency of occurrence spans from 1.46% in MM to 27.53% in lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC).
evidence: Supported by data analysis

claim: In pancreatic adenocarcinoma, esophageal adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, colorectal adenocarcinoma and skin cutaneous melanoma, the frequency of TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations was higher than 6%.
source: Notably, in pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PAAD), esophageal adenocarcinoma (ESAD), squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC), colorectal adenocarcinoma (COAD) and skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM), the frequency of TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations was higher than 6% (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by data analysis in Supplementary file 1

claim: In lung small cell carcinoma, despite nearly ubiquitous presence of TP53 alterations, there were no exon-6 truncations found.
source: This phenomenon is best exemplified by our observations of lung small cell carcinoma (LUSCC) wherein, despite the nearly ubiquitous presence of TP53 alterations, we found no exon-6 truncations (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data analysis shown in figures

claim: There is a statistically significant increase in the frequency of TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations in colorectal cancer metastatic site tumors compared to primary tumors in the MSKCC cohort.
source: Strikingly, in the MSKCC cohort, we found a statistically significant increase in the frequency of TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations in colorectal cancer (CRC) metastatic site tumors with respect to primary tumors (Figure 1G and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1G

claim: A previous study showed an increased representation of TP53 exon-6 mutations in liver metastases of colorectal cancers.
source: This is reminiscent of a previous study in which an analysis of colorectal cancers revealed an increased representation of TP53 exon-6 mutations in liver metastases (Miyaki et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miyaki et al., 2002

claim: p53 C-terminal truncating proteins ectopically expressed in H1299 cells failed to decrease cell viability.
source: As it is consistent with their lack of tumor suppressor activities, different p53 C-terminal truncating proteins ectopically expressed in a p53 homozygous deletion cell line (H1299) failed to decrease cell viability (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Ectopic expression of TP53 exon-6 truncations in A549 cells induced changes in morphological appearances.
source: Yet, as shown in Figure 2, ectopic expression of TP53 exon-6 truncations in A549 cell line (lung cancer-derived epithelial line) induced changes in the morphological appearances of cells (Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Ectopic expression of TP53 exon-6 truncations in A549 cells induced the transition of filamentous actin from cortical distribution to stress fibers formation.
source: and the acquisition of mesenchymal-like features such as (i) the transition of filamentous actin from a cortical distribution to stress fibers formation (Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Ectopic expression of TP53 exon-6 truncations in A549 cells decreased expression and localization of E-cadherin.
source: (ii) decreased expression and localization of E-cadherin (Figure 2D and E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D and 2E

claim: Ectopic expression of TP53 exon-6 truncations in A549 cells increased expression of vimentin.
source: (iii) increased expression of vimentin
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Ectopic expression of TP53 exon-6 truncations in A549 cells increased expression of EMT master regulators Slug, Snail and Zeb1.
source: and (iv) increased expression of the master regulators of epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT): Slug, Snail and Zeb1 (Figure 2E) (Lamouille et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and citation

claim: Cells expressing p53 exon-6 truncations were characterized by increased motility.
source: Consistent with an EMT-like phenotype, cells expressing p53 exon-6 truncations were also characterized by increased motility (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Cells expressing p53 exon-6 truncations were characterized by increased extra-cellular matrix invasion.
source: and extra-cellular matrix invasion (Figure 2G) (Lamouille et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and citation

claim: B16-F1 melanoma cells expressing p53 R213* mutant showed a dramatic increase in the number of melanoma colonies in lung at day 14 post-injection in mice.
source: As shown in Figure 2H and I and Figure 2—figure supplement 4, at day 14 post-injection, we observed a dramatic increase in the number of melanoma colonies in lung in the case of cells expressing the p53 R213* mutant.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2H, 2I, and supplement

claim: Not all premature truncating transcripts undergo nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD).
source: Yet, it has been shown that not all premature truncating transcripts undergo NMD, and that variation in NMD efficiency among different tissues, cell types and even individuals could lead to the expression of variable amounts of truncated proteins that could impact the clinical presentation and outcome of diseases.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about NMD

claim: No NMD-mediated mRNA diminution was observed in lymphoblasts and bone cells of patients carrying premature termination codons in the collagen X gene.
source: For example, no NMD-mediated mRNA diminution was observed in the lymphoblasts and bone cells of patients carrying premature termination codons in the collagen X gene (Bateman et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bateman et al., 2003

claim: Analysis of TCGA tumor samples indicated a comparable, though slightly decreased, expression of RNA transcripts harboring TP53 truncating mutations compared to all p53 mRNAs.
source: Analysis of four individual sequencing studies done by the TCGA project indicated a large distribution in the expression of all p53 mRNAs and a comparable, though slightly decreased, expression of RNA transcripts harboring TP53 truncating mutations (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by data analysis shown in figures and supplementary file

claim: p53 exon-6 truncating mutants were expressed in SW684, Calu-6 and DMS114 cell extracts.
source: As shown in Figure 3C and in Figure 3—figure supplement 3, we observed that p53 exon-6 truncating mutants were indeed expressed in the SW684, Calu-6 and DMS114 cell extracts.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in figures

claim: The bands detected by western blot analysis corresponded to distinct p53 mutant forms as verified by p53 knockdown.
source: Notably, analyses of p53 expression upon knockdown with two independent p53 small hairpin RNAs (shRNA) verified that the bands we detected by western blot analysis corresponded to distinct p53 mutant forms (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental validation shown in figures

claim: Acute inactivation of p53 in cells expressing R213* and R196* mutants resulted in down-regulation of EMT markers and up-regulation of E-cadherin.
source: Acute inactivation of p53 (i.e., 2–4 days) with two independent p53 shRNAs in cells that exclusively expressed the p53 R213* and R196* mutants resulted in a down-regulation of EMT markers and up-regulation of E-cadherin (Figure 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures

claim: Prolonged inactivation of p53 in tumor-derived cell lines harboring TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations resulted in a dramatic decrease in cell viability.
source: Yet, prolonged inactivation (i.e., more than 6 days) of p53 in tumor-derived cell lines harboring TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations resulted in a dramatic decrease in the viability of the cells over time (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3E and 3F

claim: The decreased number of cells upon p53 knockdown was due to an increase in cell death as measured by cleaved-PARP levels.
source: We confirmed that the decreased number of cells we found in our viability assay was due to an increase in cell death by measuring levels of expression of the apoptotic marker cleaved-PARP upon p53 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figure

claim: Silencing p53 in cell lines harboring wild type p53, hotspot missense mutants, longer truncations, shorter truncations, or p53 homozygous deletion did not affect the number of viable cells.
source: This appeared to be unique to cells expressing the R213* and R196* exon-6 truncating mutations (SW684, DMS114 and Calu-6) as silencing p53 in cell lines harboring (i) a wild type p53 allele (A549 and MCF7 cells), (ii) a 'hotspot' missense p53 mutant (AU565), (iii) a longer truncation (HCC1937), (iv) a shorter truncation (H2126), or (v) a p53 homozygous deletion (H1299) did not affect the number of viable cells (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3F and 3G

claim: Inactivation of p53 using inducible CRISPR-Cas9 resulted in a substantial decrease in cell viability only in cells expressing TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations.
source: In these cases, the inactivation of p53 also resulted in a substantial decrease in cell viability only in those cells expressing TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using CRISPR-Cas9 system

claim: p53-psi is a naturally occurring alternative splice isoform generated by the use of an alternative cryptic splicing acceptor site in intron-6 with an approximate molecular weight of 35 kDa.
source: p53-psi is a naturally occurring alternative splice isoform generated by the use of an alternative cryptic splicing acceptor site in intron-6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) with an approximate molecular weight of 35 kDa.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and figure reference

claim: A p53-psi like protein can be generated by mutations occurring at the splice acceptor site in exon-7 (Hop62, c.673–2A>G TP53 mutation).
source: As demonstrated in Senturk et al., a p53-psi like protein can also be generated by mutations occurring at the splice acceptor site in exon-7 (Hop62, c.673–2A>G TP53 mutation).
evidence: Supported by citation to Senturk et al.

claim: p53 exon-6 truncating mutants lack most of the domains required for p53 canonical tumor suppressor activities (nuclear localization, oligomerization domains, and the alpha helix required for p53-DNA binding).
source: Like p53-psi, these p53 mutants lack most of the domains required for p53 canonical tumor suppressor activities (i.e., nuclear localization, oligomerization domains, and the alpha helix required for p53-DNA binding)
evidence: Based on structural analysis and inference from p53-psi similarity

claim: p53 exon-6 truncating mutants are excluded from the nucleus.
source: Therefore, unsurprisingly, we not only found that p53 exon-6 truncating mutants were excluded from the nucleus (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B

claim: p53 exon-6 truncating mutants lack transcriptional activities.
source: but also that they lacked transcriptional activities (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4C

claim: p53-WT can localize to the mitochondria and bind to Cyclophilin D under stress conditions through a domain present from amino acid 80 to amino acid 220.
source: Previous studies have indicated that p53-WT under stress conditions could localize to the mitochondria and bind to the mitochondria permeability transition pore (MPTP) regulator Cyclophilin D (CypD) through a domain present from amino acid 80 to amino acid 220 of the p53 protein (Vaseva et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vaseva et al., 2012

claim: p53-psi is constitutively localized to the mitochondria where it binds to CypD.
source: More recently Senturk et al., showed that p53-psi is constitutively localized to the mitochondria where it also binds to CypD.
evidence: Supported by citation to Senturk et al.

claim: The tumor promoting activities of p53-psi require its molecular and functional interaction with CypD.
source: Specifically, they were able to demonstrate that the tumor promoting activities of p53-psi requires its molecular and functional interaction with CypD (Senturk et al., 2014) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Senturk et al., 2014

claim: CypD is a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase and the only validated regulatory component of the MPTP.
source: CypD is a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase and the only validated regulatory component of the MPTP (Baines et al., 2005; Schinzel et al., 2005; Giorgio et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: CypD activity can be pharmacologically inactivated by Cyclosporin A (CsA).
source: CypD activity can be pharmacologically inactivated by Cyclosporin A (CsA).
evidence: Supported by established pharmacological knowledge

claim: CsA was initially isolated from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum.
source: CsA was initially isolated from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum (Heusler and Pletscher, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Heusler and Pletscher, 2001

claim: CsA is an immunosuppressant drug that reduces the activity of the immune system by interfering with the activity and growth of T cells.
source: It is best known as an immunosuppressant drug that reduces the activity of the immune system by interfering with the activity and growth of T cells (Bunjes et al., 1981).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bunjes et al., 1981

claim: CsA is a potent inhibitor of CypD by preventing the binding of CypD to other components of the MPTP.
source: In addition to its effect on T cells, CsA has also been shown to be a potent inhibitor of CypD by preventing the binding of CypD to other components of the MPTP (Halestrap and Davidson, 1990, Nicolli et al., 1996; Baines et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: p53 exon-6 truncating mutants were partially localized to the mitochondria.
source: We found that p53 exon-6 truncating mutants were partially localized to the mitochondria (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in figures

claim: p53 exon-6 truncating mutants could bind to CypD in the mitochondrial fractions.
source: and, as shown by our immunoprecipitation experiments, could bind to CypD in the mitochondrial fractions (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4E

claim: The binding of p53 exon-6 truncating mutants with CypD was not due to changes in the expression of CypD.
source: The binding of p53 exon-6 truncating mutants with CypD was not due to changes in the expression of CypD, as neither the ectopic expression of TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations nor decreasing their expression had any effects on CypD expression or its mitochondrial localization (Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures

claim: Knockdown of CypD in cells expressing p53-psi or exon-6 truncating mutants did not affect the localization of truncated p53 isoforms to mitochondria.
source: Similarly, knockdown of CypD in cells expressing p53-psi or exon-6 truncating mutants did not affect the localization of truncated p53 isoforms to mitochondria (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figure

claim: Cells ectopically expressing p53-psi and the R196* and R213* mutants showed increased permeability of the MPTP.
source: We found an increased permeability of the MPTP only in the case of p53-psi and the R196* and R213* mutants.
evidence: Supported by calcein fluorescence assay data

claim: Cells expressing the W146* p53 mutant showed a decrease of MPTP permeability.
source: Interestingly, in the cells expressing the W146* p53 mutants we instead observed a decrease of MPTP permeability (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by calcein fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 4F

claim: In the presence of CsA, the increase in pore permeability observed in cells expressing R196*, R213* p53 exon-6 mutants and p53-psi was completely ablated.
source: We found that in the presence of CsA, the increase in the pore permeability that we observed in cells expressing R196*, R213* p53 exon-6 mutants and p53-psi was completely ablated (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with CsA treatment shown in Figure 4F

claim: Only cells expressing p53-psi and exon-6 truncating mutations showed a decrease in mitochondrial permeability after knockdown of p53.
source: As shown in Figure 4G, only cells expressing p53-psi and exon-6 truncating mutations showed a decrease in mitochondrial permeability after the knockdown of p53.
evidence: Supported by calcein fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 4G

claim: CypD silencing resulted in a decrease in mitochondrial permeability only in cells expressing p53-psi and exon-6 truncating mutations.
source: Similarly, CypD silencing resulted in a decrease in mitochondrial permeability only in those cells expressing p53-psi and exon-6 truncating mutations (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figure

claim: Knockdown of p53 or CypD in cell lines expressing p53-psi and exon-6 truncating mutations resulted in hyperpolarization of mitochondria.
source: As shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B, knockdown of p53 or CypD in cell lines expressing p53-psi and exon-6 truncating mutations specifically resulted in the hyperpolarization of mitochondria.
evidence: Supported by JC-1 assay data shown in figures

claim: Short-term inactivation of CypD led to a decrease in mesenchymal markers in cells expressing p53-psi or exon-6 truncating mutants.
source: Figure 5A demonstrates that short-term inactivation of CypD led to a decrease in mesenchymal markers in cells specifically expressing p53-psi or exon-6 truncating mutants (Hop62, DMS114 and Calu-6).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A

claim: CypD long-term knockdown led to a reduction in viable cells in in-vitro cell viability experiments.
source: When p53 was inactivated in these cells, we observed a reduction in cell viability; analogously, CypD long-term knockdown also led to a reduction in viable cells in in-vitro cell viability experiments (Figure 5C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assay data shown in figures

claim: Treatment of cells with the CypD inhibitor C-9 resulted in reduced cell viability.
source: This result was also recapitulated by treatment of cells with the novel CypD inhibitor, C-9 (Figure 5B) (Valasani et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by drug treatment data shown in Figure 5B and citation

claim: Inactivation of CypD expression in xenograft models using inducible CRISPR-Cas9 decreased the tumor volume of p53 exon-6 truncating mutant-expressing cells (Calu6), but not p53-WT expressing cells (A549).
source: Figure 5E and F show that the inactivation of CypD expression in xenograft models using an inducible CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing system decreased the tumor volume of p53 exon-6 truncating mutant-expressing cells (Calu6), but not the tumor volume of p53-WT expressing cells (A549) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by in vivo xenograft data shown in Figures 5E, 5F, and supplement

claim: TP53 mutations produce a multiplicity of alleles with diverse activities that contribute differently to tumorigenesis.
source: In summary, our analysis of human tumors, combined with the detailed molecular characterization of TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations, offers strong support for the idea that chromosome 17p deletions and, particularly, TP53 mutations produce a multiplicity of alleles with diverse activities that contribute differently to tumorigenesis by providing distinct, selective advantages (Petitjean et al., 2007; Brosh and Rotter, 2009; Olivier et al., 2010; Oren and Rotter, 2010; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by the study's findings and citations to previous work

claim: p53 exon-6 truncating mutants are uniquely able to activate a pro-tumorigenic cellular program.
source: Our studies, in fact, revealed that p53 exon-6 truncating mutants not only lack transcriptional activities and the capacity to respond to DNA damage, but are also uniquely able to activate a pro-tumorigenic cellular program.
evidence: Supported by experimental findings in the study

claim: TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations are highly abundant and are enriched in certain tumors.
source: Consistent with the capabilities of these p53 mutants to promote rather than halt tumorigenesis, TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations are highly abundant and are enriched in certain tumors (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1

claim: The higher than expected frequency of TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations could be explained by a specific etiology and/or a particular mutagenic modality.
source: Although, in principle this implies that these specific mutants could increase the fitness of tumors, we cannot exclude the possibility that the higher than expected frequency we observed in tumors could alternatively be explained by a specific etiology and/or a particular mutagenic modality.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about alternative explanations

claim: p53 exon-6 truncating mutants are similar to the naturally occurring p53 isoform p53-psi.
source: One interesting feature of the p53 exon-6 truncating mutants is their similarity to the naturally occurring p53 isoform p53-psi.
evidence: Based on structural and functional comparisons in the study

claim: Inhibition of CypD activity reduces mitochondrial permeability and induces changes in mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Inhibition of CypD activity, either genetically or pharmacologically, has been reported to reduce mitochondrial permeability and induce changes in mitochondrial membrane potential.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and citations

claim: Cells expressing TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations are proliferating under normal conditions and are dependent on CypD for their survival.
source: Yet, cells expressing TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations are proliferating under normal conditions and are actually dependent on CypD for their survival.
evidence: Supported by experimental findings in the study

claim: The MPTP has a role not only in inducing cell death under cellular stress, but also in physiological processes.
source: These observations are consistent with more recent reports indicating that the MPTP has a role not only in inducing cell death under cellular stress, but also in physiological processes (Kwong and Molkentin, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kwong and Molkentin, 2015

claim: The MPTP has a role in the induction of phenotypic changes associated with pro-metastatic features.
source: and in the induction of phenotypic changes associated with pro-metastatic features (Senturk et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Senturk et al., 2014

claim: TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations are distinguished from other p53 gain of function mutants by their requirement of mitochondria localization, interaction with CypD, and lack of transcriptional activities.
source: The requirement of mitochondria localization, interaction with CypD and the lack of transcriptional activities distinguish TP53 exon-6 truncating mutations from other p53 gain of function mutants with pro-tumorigenic functions (e.g. R175, G245, R248, R249, R273 and R282).
evidence: Based on comparative analysis of different p53 mutants in the study

claim: p53 gain of function mutants' activities strongly depend on their nuclear localization and transcriptional activities.
source: Despite the fact that p53 gain of function mutants are also capable of inducing pro-metastatic features, we found that their activities strongly depend on their nuclear localization and transcriptional activities.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about p53 gain of function mutants

claim: The p53 W146* mutant is unable to interact with CypD despite its ability to localize to the mitochondria.
source: In our study, structure-function analysis has also shown that the p53 W146* mutant is unable to interact with CypD despite its ability to localize to the mitochondria.
evidence: Supported by experimental findings in the study

claim: The expression of the p53 W146* mutant increased the expression of E-cadherin.
source: Interestingly and contrary to p53-psi and p53 exon-6 truncating mutants, the expression of the p53 W146* mutant increased the expression of E-cadherin instead of reducing it (Figure 2D and E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D and 2E

claim: The p53 W146* mutant may interact with other components of the MPTP and antagonize the function of CypD.
source: To explain this observation, it is tempting to speculate that the p53 W146* mutant may interact with other components of the MPTP and antagonize the function of CypD.
evidence: Speculative reasoning to explain observations

claim: Cancer cells harboring exon-6 TP53 truncating mutations have selective dependencies to CypD activity.
